title: The solar system: eight planets, one Sun, and Earth is one of them

summary.text: The Earth is a planet. It is one of eight planets that go round the Sun. In order from the Sun, they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The first four are small and rocky. The last four are giants, made mostly of gas and ice. All eight are lit and warmed by the same Sun. Its light spreads out as it travels, so the further a planet is, the weaker its sunlight. Neptune gets about 900 times less sunlight than the Earth. The Earth is at a distance where water can stay liquid, and that is part of why life could begin here.
summary.art: The Sun on the left with eight planets in a row going right, small rocky ones close in and big giants far out, the blue Earth third from the Sun with a tiny label 'You are here'.

intro.hook: Stand in a sunny patch by a window and hold out your hand. Feel the warmth. That warmth came from the Sun. The same Sun is shining on seven other planets right now. Do they all feel the same warmth as your hand?
intro.text: In this unit you find out. You meet the eight planets and learn that the Earth is one of them. With a phone torch and a sheet of squared paper, you measure how light spreads out as it travels. That test shows why Mercury is scorching and Neptune is freezing and dark. You also hear how Galileo looked at Venus through a telescope and found that not everything goes round the Earth.
intro.art: A child's hand held out in a patch of sunlight on a tiled floor, with a window behind and a faint row of eight planets drawn in the sky outside.

outcomes: I can name the eight planets in order from the Sun, and say that the Earth is the third planet.
I can say what makes something a planet, and why Pluto is now called a dwarf planet.
I can run a fair test that shows how light spreads out with distance, and use it to explain why far planets are cold and dim.
I can explain why the planets keep going round the Sun, and why a planet further out takes longer to go round once.
I can tell how Galileo's view of Venus in 1610 showed that not everything goes round the Earth.
I can sort the planets into rocky planets and giant planets, and say how the two kinds differ.

terms.meaning: The Sun and everything that goes round it: eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets.
terms.example: The Earth and the Moon are both part of the solar system.
terms.art: The Sun in the middle with the paths of eight planets drawn as rings round it.

terms.meaning: A big, round world that goes round a star and has cleared its path of other big things. A planet does not make its own light. It shines only because sunlight falls on it.
terms.example: The Earth, Mars and Jupiter are planets.
terms.art: A round planet half lit by sunlight coming from one side, with its dark half facing away.

terms.meaning: A huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light and heat. The Sun is a star.
terms.example: The Sun is the nearest star to the Earth.
terms.art: A glowing yellow ball with rays, labelled 'the Sun, our star'.

terms.meaning: The path one thing takes as it goes round another in space. An orbit is also the word for going round.
terms.example: The Earth orbits the Sun once a year.
terms.art: A dotted oval path round the Sun with a small Earth on it and an arrow showing the way it moves.

terms.meaning: The force that pulls things towards each other. Big things like the Sun pull very strongly.
terms.example: Gravity makes a dropped spoon fall to the floor. The Sun's gravity holds the Earth in its orbit.
terms.art: A spoon falling from a hand to a kitchen floor, and beside it the Sun with a faint arrow pulling the Earth inwards.

terms.meaning: The time a planet takes to go round the Sun once.
terms.example: A year on the Earth is about 365 days. A year on Mars is 687 Earth days.
terms.art: A calendar page next to the Earth going once round the Sun.

terms.meaning: A planet with a hard surface of rock and metal that you could stand on. The four planets nearest the Sun are rocky.
terms.example: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky planets.
terms.art: Four small planets in a row with rocky, cratered or cloudy surfaces.

terms.meaning: A very big planet made mostly of gas, or of gas and ice, with no hard surface to stand on. The four planets furthest from the Sun are giants.
terms.example: Jupiter is a giant planet. More than 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
terms.art: Jupiter with its stripes, Saturn with its rings, and blue Uranus and Neptune, all huge next to a tiny Earth.

terms.meaning: A round world that goes round the Sun but shares its path with many other icy or rocky things. It has not cleared its path.
terms.example: Pluto has been called a dwarf planet since 2006.
terms.art: Small icy Pluto among many little rocks and ice lumps far from the Sun.

terms.meaning: A lump of rock or metal that goes round the Sun. Asteroids are much smaller than planets, and most are not round.
terms.example: Most asteroids go round the Sun in a wide ring between Mars and Jupiter, called the asteroid belt.
terms.art: A lumpy, potato-shaped rock in space with craters on it.

terms.meaning: The layer of gas, or air, that wraps round a planet.
terms.example: The Earth's atmosphere is the air we breathe. Venus has a very thick atmosphere that traps heat.
terms.art: The Earth with a thin glowing blue layer round its edge.

terms.meaning: A tube with lenses or mirrors that makes faraway things look bigger and clearer.
terms.example: Galileo used a telescope in 1610 to look at Venus and Jupiter.
terms.art: An old-fashioned long telescope on a stand pointed at the night sky.

terms.meaning: The different shapes a lit ball seems to have, depending on how much of its lit half we can see.
terms.example: The Moon shows phases from crescent to full. Venus shows phases too, seen through a telescope.
terms.art: A row of Venus shapes from a big thin crescent to a small full circle.

terms.meaning: A machine built to travel in space. A spacecraft with no people on board is often called a probe.
terms.example: India's Mangalyaan spacecraft went into orbit round Mars in 2014.
terms.art: A small spacecraft with a gold body and one big solar panel flying near a red planet.

explanations.definition: A planet is a big, round world that goes round the Sun and has cleared its path of other big things. The Earth does all three, so the Earth is a planet.
explanations.description: From the ground, the Earth feels flat and still, and the planets look like bright dots. So for a long time, most people thought the Earth was a different kind of thing from the planets. It is not. The Earth goes round the Sun, just as Mars and Jupiter do. Like them, it shines only with sunlight that bounces off it. Seen from Mars, the Earth looks like a bright blue-white dot in the sky. The Earth is the third planet from the Sun. It is the biggest of the four rocky planets.
examples: Photos taken by spacecraft near Mars show the Earth as a small bright dot.
In the evening sky, Venus looks like a very bright star. Someone on Venus would see the Earth as a bright dot too.
The Earth takes about 365 days to go round the Sun once. That is one year.
explanations.art: The view from the rocky surface of Mars at dusk, with a tiny blue dot shining low in the sky and a label 'Earth'.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: the ground under your feet belongs to a planet.

explanations.definition: In order from the Sun, the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
explanations.description: One way to remember the order is a sentence where each word starts with the planet's first letter: 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming.' The four inner planets are close together, near the Sun. Then there is a wide gap with the asteroid belt in it. The four outer planets are very far apart. Neptune is about 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is. If the Earth were 10 centimetres from the Sun, Neptune would be 3 metres away.
examples: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun.
Jupiter is the biggest planet. Saturn has the brightest rings.
Uranus spins tipped over on its side, so it seems to roll round the Sun.
explanations.art: A long strip with the Sun at one end and the eight planets marked at their real spacing, the first four bunched up near the Sun.
explanations.context: This card lists the eight planets in order and shows how far apart they are.

explanations.definition: The four planets nearest the Sun are small and made of rock and metal. The four furthest planets are giants made mostly of gas, or of gas and ice.
explanations.description: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars have hard ground you could stand on. Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium gas, the same gases the Sun is made of. Uranus and Neptune have a lot of water, ammonia and methane as well, mostly as hot, thick fluids deep inside, under thick air. None of the four giants has a hard surface to land on. Going down into one, the gas just gets thicker and hotter. All four giants have rings, though only Saturn's are bright enough to see easily with a small telescope.
examples: Mars is red because its rocks and dust contain rusty iron.
Jupiter has a giant storm, the Great Red Spot, that is wider than the whole Earth.
Saturn is so light for its size that, on average, it is less heavy than the same amount of water.
explanations.art: The four rocky planets on one side, small and solid, and the four giants on the other side, huge, striped and ringed.
explanations.context: This card sorts the planets into two families: the small rocky ones and the giants.

explanations.concept: Light spreads out as it travels
explanations.definition: Light from a small source spreads out in all directions. Twice as far away, the same light covers four times the area, so each part of it gets a quarter as much light.
explanations.description: In the torch test, the light through a small square hole made a square patch on the paper. When the paper was twice as far away, the patch was twice as wide and twice as tall. So it covered four times as many squares, and it looked dimmer. The Sun's light spreads out in the same way. Jupiter is about 5 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is. 5 times 5 is 25, so sunlight at Jupiter is about 25 times weaker than here. Neptune is about 30 times as far. 30 times 30 is 900, so Neptune gets about 900 times less sunlight. On Neptune at noon, the Sun would look like a dazzling tiny star.
examples: Mercury gets about 7 times as much sunlight as the Earth.
Mars gets a little less than half as much sunlight as the Earth.
A spacecraft going to Jupiter needs much bigger solar panels than one near the Earth.
explanations.art: Beams from the Sun spreading out like a widening cone, falling on one square near the Sun, four squares further out and nine squares further still.
explanations.context: This card explains what the torch test showed, and what it means for planets far from the Sun.

explanations.concept: Why the Earth has liquid water
explanations.definition: The Earth is at a distance from the Sun where water can stay liquid on its surface. Its air keeps it a little warmer, too.
explanations.description: Close to the Sun, sunlight is so strong that water boils away. Far from the Sun, sunlight is so weak that water freezes solid. The Earth is in between, where water can be liquid. Distance is not the whole story, though. A planet's air matters too. Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury, but Venus is the hottest planet. Its very thick air traps the heat, so its ground is about 460 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. The Earth's thinner air keeps us warm enough without cooking us. Every living thing we know of lives on the Earth.
examples: Mars once had rivers and lakes. Today its water is frozen at its poles and under its ground.
Mercury has almost no air, so its night side gets colder than the coldest place on Earth.
Some moons of Jupiter and Saturn, like Europa and Enceladus, probably have oceans of liquid water under thick ice, kept liquid by their own inner heat.
explanations.art: Three bowls of water: one near a fierce Sun boiling, one far away frozen, and one in the middle, labelled Earth, with fish swimming.
explanations.context: This card explains why the Earth can have rivers, rain and oceans, and why other planets mostly cannot.

explanations.concept: Why the planets keep going round the Sun
explanations.definition: Each planet is moving forwards very fast. The Sun's gravity pulls it inwards all the time. Together, these bend the planet's path into an orbit round the Sun.
explanations.description: Something that is moving keeps going in a straight line unless a force changes its path. In the marble test, the rim of the plate pushed the marble inwards and kept it going round. At the gap, nothing pushed any more, and the marble rolled off in a straight line. The Sun's gravity does the job of the rim for the planets, though it pulls without touching. If the Sun's gravity suddenly stopped, every planet would fly off in a straight line. The Earth moves at about 30 kilometres every second as it goes round the Sun.
examples: Swing a sock tied to a string in a circle. Let go, and it flies off in a straight line.
The Moon stays in orbit round the Earth because of the Earth's gravity.
Spacecraft use the same idea. Rockets give them enough speed, and gravity bends their path.
explanations.art: A planet moving along its curved path, with an arrow pointing straight ahead for its motion and an arrow pointing to the Sun for gravity.
explanations.context: This card explains what keeps the planets on their paths. The marble-and-plate test shows the same idea.

explanations.concept: Planets further out take longer to go round
explanations.definition: A planet's year is the time it takes to go round the Sun once. The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year.
explanations.description: There are two reasons. A planet further out has a much longer path to travel. It also moves more slowly, because the Sun's gravity is weaker out there. Mercury, the closest planet, goes round in just 88 days. Neptune, the furthest, takes about 165 Earth years. Neptune was discovered in 1846, and it finished its first full orbit since then only in 2011. In 1619 Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer, found an exact rule linking a planet's distance to the length of its year.
examples: A year on Mars is 687 Earth days, almost two of our years.
Jupiter takes about 12 Earth years to go round the Sun once.
A child who is 8 on the Earth has not yet lived one Saturn year, which is about 29 and a half Earth years.
explanations.art: Eight planets on their orbits, with small numbers beside each: 88 days, 225 days, 365 days, 687 days, 12 years, 29 years, 84 years, 165 years.
explanations.context: This card explains why a year is a different length on each planet.

explanations.concept: How the solar system was born
explanations.description: Most scientists think the solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge, slowly spinning cloud of gas and dust. Gravity pulled most of the cloud into the middle, where it became the Sun. The rest flattened into a spinning disc round the young Sun. In the disc, dust and ice stuck together into bigger and bigger lumps, and some lumps grew into planets. Near the Sun, it was too warm for ice to stay frozen, so only rock and metal could clump. That is why the inner planets are rocky. Further out, ice could freeze too, so planets grew bigger and pulled in lots of gas. This idea explains a lot. All the planets go round the Sun the same way, in nearly the same flat plane. Telescopes have also photographed discs like this round young stars. But many details are still being worked out, such as how fast Jupiter grew.
examples: The oldest rocks found in meteorites are about 4.6 billion years old.
In 2014, a telescope in Chile photographed a young star called HL Tauri with a dusty disc and dark rings in it.
All eight planets orbit the Sun in the same direction.
explanations.art: A flat, spinning disc of glowing dust round a bright young Sun, with small lumps clumping together in it.
explanations.context: This card tells the best idea scientists have for how the Sun and planets began. It is well supported, but not every part is settled.

explanations.description: Pluto was found in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, a young American astronomer, and was called the ninth planet for 76 years. Then astronomers found more and more icy worlds out near Pluto. In 2005 they found Eris, which is about as big as Pluto. Were all of these planets? In 2006 the International Astronomical Union, the world group of astronomers, voted on a definition. A planet must go round the Sun, be round, and have cleared its path of other big things. Pluto shares its path with many icy worlds, so it was called a dwarf planet. Not everyone agrees.
examples: Pluto is smaller than our Moon.
The New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015 and found mountains of ice and a heart-shaped plain.
Ceres, the biggest object in the asteroid belt, is also called a dwarf planet.

perspectives.explanation: A planet must have cleared its path. Pluto has not, so it is a dwarf planet. This keeps the list of planets to eight clear, different kinds of world.

perspectives.who: Alan Stern, the scientist who led the New Horizons mission, and others who study planets' surfaces
perspectives.explanation: A planet should be any world big enough for its own gravity to pull it round. By that rule, Pluto is a planet, and so are Eris and some big moons. Where a world goes round should not decide what it is.

explanations.art: Small icy Pluto with its heart-shaped plain, and two speech bubbles from two astronomers: 'dwarf planet' and 'planet'.
explanations.context: Pluto used to be called the ninth planet. This card is about a real argument among astronomers about what a planet is.

explanations.concept: Is there a hidden ninth planet?
explanations.description: Far beyond Neptune, a few small icy worlds have long, stretched orbits that seem to point roughly the same way. In 2016 two astronomers, Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown, said this could be caused by the gravity of an unseen planet, perhaps several times as heavy as the Earth. Nobody has found it yet. Other astronomers think the pattern is only chance. We have spotted just a few of these far worlds, mostly in parts of the sky that are easier to search.
examples: Neptune itself was found in 1846 in a similar way. Urbain Le Verrier, a French mathematician, worked out where it must be from the way it tugged on Uranus.
A very far, dim planet would reflect very little sunlight, which is why it would be so hard to see.
A new telescope in Chile, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, is searching the sky and may settle the question.

perspectives.who: Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown, in 2016
perspectives.explanation: The far icy worlds line up too neatly to be chance. A big unseen planet is pulling them into line.
We have found only a handful of these worlds, so the pattern may come from where we happened to look. More searching is needed before anyone says there is a planet.

explanations.art: A dark, faint planet drawn with a dotted outline far beyond Neptune, with a few small icy worlds on long stretched paths round it.
explanations.context: This card is about an open question: could there be a planet in our solar system that nobody has seen yet?

agreed.text: The Earth and seven other planets go round the Sun.
agreed.evidence: Planet positions worked out this way match what telescopes see, and spacecraft are flown to other planets using these orbits.

agreed.text: The Sun holds about 998 parts out of every 1,000 of all the matter in the solar system.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers weigh the Sun by how fast the planets go round it. Its gravity is far stronger than all the planets put together.

agreed.text: Sunlight gets weaker with distance: twice as far, a quarter as strong.
agreed.evidence: Spacecraft measure the sunlight falling on their panels as they travel out, and it drops exactly this way. The torch test shows the same at home.

agreed.text: The Earth is the only place where life is known to exist.
agreed.evidence: Spacecraft have searched Mars, Venus and the Moon closely. They have found no sign of life yet, though the search goes on.

agreed.text: The Sun and the planets formed together about 4.6 billion years ago.
agreed.evidence: The oldest meteorites, rocks that fell from space, are about this old when dated by their natural radioactivity.

challenging.claim: The Earth is the centre, and the Sun and planets go round it.
challenging.who: Most people in many lands for thousands of years, and the Greek-Egyptian astronomer Ptolemy, about 150 CE
challenging.for: The Sun, the Moon and the stars all seem to travel across our sky every day. We do not feel the Earth moving.
challenging.against: Galileo saw Venus change from a small full disc to a big thin crescent, which only fits if Venus goes round the Sun. Later measurements showed the Earth moves too.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest idea about the planets, and how it was shown wrong.

challenging.who: Astronomers until 2006, and some planet scientists today
challenging.for: Pluto is round, has its own moons, mountains and air, and goes round the Sun.
challenging.against: Pluto shares its path with many other icy worlds, and Eris is about as big. The 2006 rule says a planet must clear its path.
challenging.context: This card is about whether Pluto should be called a planet.

challenging.claim: The planets closest to the Sun are always the hottest.
challenging.for: Sunlight is strongest close to the Sun, as the torch test shows.
challenging.against: Venus is hotter than Mercury, though it is further from the Sun, because its thick air traps the heat.
challenging.context: This card is about a natural guess that is mostly right but has one big exception.

challenging.claim: The planets are spread out evenly.
challenging.who: A common idea, because pictures in books often show them evenly spaced
challenging.for: Drawings in books fit the planets into one page, at equal gaps.
challenging.against: The four inner planets are packed close to the Sun. Neptune is about 30 times as far out as the Earth. Real spacing would not fit on a book page.
challenging.context: This card is about how book pictures can mislead us about the solar system.

challenging.claim: There is a ninth planet beyond Neptune that we have not seen.
challenging.for: Some far icy worlds have orbits that seem to line up, as if something big were pulling them.
challenging.against: Nobody has seen it, and the pattern may come from where astronomers happened to look.
challenging.context: This card is about a planet that may or may not exist.

big_questions.q: We call the Earth 'down here' and the planets 'up there'. If you stood on Mars, where would the Earth be?
big_questions.hint: Up in the Martian sky, as a bright dot. Is 'up there' a place, or does it depend on where you stand?

big_questions.q: All eight planets get light from the same Sun. Why are they so different from each other?
big_questions.hint: Think about the torch test. What changes with distance? Then think about what each planet is made of and how much air it has.

big_questions.q: If the Earth were a little closer to the Sun, or a little further, would we be here?
big_questions.hint: Venus is a bit closer and is hot enough to melt lead. Mars is a bit further and its water is frozen.

big_questions.q: Is a planet that has not cleared its path really a different kind of thing, or did people just choose a new name?
big_questions.hint: Pluto did not change in 2006. Only the rule changed. Who gets to decide what a word means?

big_questions.q: There are probably more planets in our galaxy than stars. Is the Earth special, or one of many?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have found more than 6,000 planets round other stars, but none yet that we know has life.

big_questions.q: Everything you eat grew from sunlight that reached the Earth. How much of you came from the Sun?
big_questions.hint: Plants use sunlight to make food. You eat plants, or animals that ate plants.

story.title: One Lamp for Eight Worlds
story.note: Lakshmi, Arjun, their grandmother and this evening are made up. The facts in the story are real: the order of the planets, how sunlight weakens with distance, Venus's thick hot air, and Venus as the bright 'evening star'.
text: The power went off at seven o'clock, just as Lakshmi opened her library book. The fan slowed and stopped. The whole flat went dark, and so did every window in the building across the road in Thiruvananthapuram.

'Nobody move,' said Ammamma. Lakshmi heard her grandmother feel her way to the pooja shelf. A match scratched. A small flame grew on the wick of the brass oil lamp, and Ammamma set it on the floor in the middle of the hall.
Lakshmi was eight. Her little brother Arjun was six, and he did not like the dark. He crawled right up to the lamp and sat with his knees almost touching it.
'Not so close,' said Ammamma. 'You'll get too hot. Move back a bit.'
Arjun shuffled back one hand's width. 'It's still hot on my face,' he said. 'But I can see everything. I can see the lines on my hand.'

Lakshmi took her book to the far corner, by the balcony door. She could hardly see the page. The lamp looked like a tiny bright star from there. 'It's too dark here to read,' she said. 'And it's cold. The breeze is coming in.'

Ammamma laughed. She had taught physics at a girls' school for thirty years, and she could never let a good question go by. 'Well,' she said, 'here we have a little solar system. The lamp is the Sun. Arjun is Mercury, the planet nearest the Sun. He is roasting. And you, Lakshmi, by the door, are far-off Neptune. You are cold and in the dark.'
'But it's the same lamp,' said Arjun. 'Why is it hot for me and dark for her?'
'Good question,' said Ammamma. 'What do you think?'
Arjun frowned. 'Because she's far away?'
'Yes. But why should being far away make the light weaker? The lamp is the same lamp.'

Nobody answered. Ammamma took an old envelope and tore a small square hole in it. She held it upright near the lamp. Lakshmi held a page from her maths notebook, the one with little squares, behind it. 'Look at the light that comes through the hole. Close to the hole, it makes a small, bright patch. Now, Lakshmi, move the paper back slowly.'
The patch of light grew wider and wider. It also grew paler.
'It's the same light,' said Lakshmi slowly. 'But it's spreading out over more squares. So each square gets less.'

'Exactly,' said Ammamma. 'Light from the lamp goes out in every direction. The further it goes, the bigger the space it has to cover, so it gets thinner. The Sun's light does the same. Neptune is about thirty times as far from the Sun as we are. By the time sunlight gets there, it is spread out so thin that it is about nine hundred times weaker than here. Neptune is colder than any freezer.'
'Then which planet are we?' asked Arjun.
'You choose,' said Ammamma. 'Where would you sit to read your book without getting too hot?'

Arjun looked at Lakshmi. Lakshmi looked at Arjun. They both moved, and they met in the middle of the hall, about two arm's lengths from the lamp. It was warm, but not too hot. The page was bright enough to read.

'There,' said Ammamma. 'You are the Earth. Not too close, not too far. On the Earth, water does not boil away and it does not freeze solid. It runs in rivers and falls as rain. That is part of why there are fish and trees and children here.'
'Can I be Venus?' asked Arjun. 'Venus is next to us.'

Ammamma pulled the thick bedsheet off the sofa and wrapped it round Arjun, right up to his chin. 'Venus is a little closer to the Sun than we are,' she said, 'and Venus has very thick air all round her. The air traps the heat like this sheet.'
'I'm boiling!' said Arjun, and threw the sheet off.
'So is Venus,' said Ammamma. 'Her ground is hot enough to melt lead. She is even hotter than Mercury, though Mercury is closer to the Sun.'

Just then the fan whirred and the lights came back on. Lakshmi ran to the balcony. The Sun had set an hour ago, and the sky over the coconut trees was deep blue. Low in the west hung one dot, brighter than anything else in the sky.
'Ammamma, look! That bright star!'

'That's not a star,' said Ammamma, coming out with the lamp still in her hand. 'That's Venus. People call her the evening star, but she makes no light of her own. You are seeing sunlight bouncing off her clouds.'
Lakshmi stared at the bright dot for a long time. 'Ammamma,' she said at last, 'if someone stood on Venus and looked this way, what would they see?'
Ammamma smiled. 'Another bright dot. A blue one. Us.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: the lamp lit everyone in the room, but its light spread out over a bigger and bigger space as it went further, so each part got less. The Sun's light does the same, which is why Mercury is scorching and Neptune is dark and frozen. The Earth is at a distance where water stays liquid. Distance is not the only thing that matters: Venus's thick air traps heat, so Venus is the hottest planet. And the Earth is not apart from the planets. Seen from Venus, the Earth is one more bright dot.
ask: Why was Arjun hot and Lakshmi cold, when they were lit by the same lamp?
What happened to the patch of light when Ammamma moved the paper further from the lamp?
Why did Ammamma wrap Arjun in a bedsheet to show what Venus is like?
Why does Venus shine so brightly if she makes no light of her own?
If someone on Venus looked at the Earth, what would they see?

games.title: Planet Top Cards
games.context: This is a card game for two or more players. Each card is a planet with three numbers. Players compare numbers to win cards, and learn the planets as they play.

printables.title: 8 planet cards to cut out
items: MERCURY. Width: 0.4 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 0.4 times the Earth's. Year: 88 days.
VENUS. Width: 0.95 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 0.7 times the Earth's. Year: 225 days.
EARTH. Width: 1 Earth. Distance from the Sun: 1. Year: 365 days.
MARS. Width: 0.5 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 1.5 times the Earth's. Year: 687 days.
JUPITER. Width: 11 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 5.2 times the Earth's. Year: about 4,330 days, almost 12 years.
SATURN. Width: 9.4 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 9.5 times the Earth's. Year: about 10,760 days, about 29 and a half years.
URANUS. Width: 4 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 19 times the Earth's. Year: about 30,690 days, about 84 years.
NEPTUNE. Width: 3.9 Earths. Distance from the Sun: 30 times the Earth's. Year: about 60,190 days, about 165 years.

rules: Shuffle the 8 cards and deal them out face down. Playing with one grown-up, each player gets 4.
The first player looks at their top card and picks one of the three: width, distance or year. They read its number aloud.
Everyone else reads the same number from their top card. The biggest number wins all the top cards.
The winner puts the won cards at the bottom of their pile and picks next.
Before reading a number, a player may guess who will win and why. A right guess with a reason earns a bonus card from the loser.
The game ends when one player has all the cards, or after 10 rounds. Whoever has most cards wins.

setup.art: Eight planet cards spread on a table, each with a drawing and three numbers.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and deal them out.

setup.art: Two players each showing a top card, Jupiter and Earth, with the word 'width' and the numbers 11 and 1 circled.
setup.caption: 2. Pick a number. The biggest number wins the cards.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 8 cards. 2. Shuffle and deal them face down.
flow.say: Each card is a planet with three numbers. You'll pick a number, and the biggest number wins.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them up. Share them out.
flow.context: This is the first step of Planet Top Cards. You cut out and deal the planet cards.

flow.do: Play rounds as in the rules. After each round, ask one question about the cards that were played.
flow.say: Jupiter won on width. Is Jupiter also the furthest planet? Which card wins on distance?
flow.kid: Pick width, distance or year. Read your number. Biggest wins!

check.q: In Planet Top Cards, which card always wins when someone picks 'year'?
options: Neptune, because it is furthest from the Sun
Jupiter, because it is the biggest
Mercury, because it is fastest
check.why: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year. Neptune is furthest, so its year is longest, about 165 Earth years. Picking Jupiter mixes up size with distance. A planet's size does not set its year.

flow.do: Lay all 8 cards in a row in order of distance.
flow.say: Let's put all the cards in order of distance. Now look at the years. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Put the cards in order of distance. Look at the years. What do you see?

good: The further out, the longer the year.
The years get longer as you go out.

games.title: Which Planet Am I?
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player secretly picks a planet. The others ask yes-or-no questions until they guess it.

printables.title: 8 secret planet cards
items: Mercury: smallest, closest to the Sun, no air, year of 88 days
Venus: hottest, thick yellow clouds, the bright evening star
Earth: liquid water, air we breathe, one Moon
Mars: red dust, frozen water, two small moons
Jupiter: biggest, stripes, the Great Red Spot storm
Saturn: bright rings, lighter for its size than water
Uranus: blue-green, spins tipped on its side
Neptune: furthest, deep blue, gets the least sunlight

printables.title: Question tally
items: Write a tick for each question asked. Fewest ticks wins.

rules: One player picks a secret planet card and doesn't show it.
The others ask questions that can be answered yes or no, such as 'Are you a giant?'
Each question gets a tick on the tally. Guess the planet in as few questions as you can.
Playing alone? Shuffle the cards face down. Read one clue at a time from the top card, and guess after each clue.

setup.art: A child holding a secret card close to her chest, while a grown-up asks a question with a thought bubble showing a ringed planet.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a secret planet. Others ask yes-or-no questions.

setup.art: A tally sheet with four ticks and the word 'Saturn!' written at the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Tick each question. Guess in as few as you can.

flow.do: Shuffle the secret planet cards. The first player picks one without showing it.
flow.say: Pick a secret planet. We'll ask questions to find out which one you are.
flow.kid: Pick a secret card. Don't show anyone!
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Planet Am I? One player picks a secret planet.

flow.do: Take turns asking yes-or-no questions and ticking the tally.
flow.say: A good first question splits the planets in half. Are you one of the four rocky planets?
flow.kid: Ask yes-or-no questions. Try to split the planets in half each time.

check.q: Which first question splits the eight planets exactly in half?
options: Are you a giant planet?
Are you Saturn?
Do you have rings that are easy to see?
check.why: Four planets are giants and four are rocky, so a yes or a no leaves exactly four. Picking 'Are you Saturn?' could win at once, but most of the time it leaves seven planets to go.

flow.do: Swap who holds the secret card and play again.
flow.say: Your turn to be the planet. Can you answer every question about your planet?
flow.kid: Now you pick a planet. Answer the questions about it.

good: Are you a giant?
Are you closer to the Sun than the Earth?

experiments.title: Light Through a Window: how does light spread out with distance?
experiments.question: When light travels twice as far, how much bigger is the patch it covers?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the squared paper is twice as far from the torch, will the patch of light cover the same number of squares, twice as many, or four times as many? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same phone torch, the same hole and the same card every time. Keep the torch and the card still. Change only one thing: how far the squared paper is from the torch. Count the squares at each distance twice, because it is easy to miss one.

materials.item: a phone with a torch
a piece of stiff card about 15 cm by 15 cm, cut from a cereal box or shoe box
scissors, for a grown-up to cut a 2 cm square hole in the middle of the card
a page from a squared maths notebook with 1 cm squares, or plain paper with 1 cm squares drawn in pencil
a ruler or school scale
a stack of books, a lump of atta dough or clay, and some tape
a room you can make dark, with the curtains closed

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the hole in the card. Do not look straight into the phone torch from close up.

schedule.what: Guess. Shine the torch through the square hole onto squared paper at 20, 30 and 40 cm. Count the lit squares. Work out what this means for the planets.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the three lit squares on squared paper, side by side, at their real sizes.
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine a phone torch through a small square hole and count how many squares of paper the light covers at different distances. It shows what happens to sunlight on its way to the planets.

setup.art: A phone standing upright against a stack of books on a table, its torch glowing, with a card with a small square hole standing 10 cm in front of it, held up by a lump of dough.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the phone up. Put the card with the hole 10 cm in front of its torch.

setup.art: A sheet of squared paper taped to a standing book, 20 cm from the torch, with a small bright square patch of light on it, and a ruler on the table showing the distance.
setup.caption: 2. Put the squared paper 20 cm from the torch. Count the lit squares.

setup.art: The same squared paper moved back to 40 cm, with a bigger, dimmer square patch of light on it, twice as wide.
setup.caption: 3. Move the paper to 30 cm, then 40 cm. Count again.

flow.do: 1. Cut a square hole 2 cm by 2 cm in the middle of the card. 2. Close the curtains and switch off the lights.
flow.say: We are going to see what happens to light as it travels further. First I'll cut a small window in this card.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a small square hole in the card. Then make the room dark.
flow.parent: A dark room makes the patch much easier to see. Evening is the easiest time. A square hole gives a square patch, which is easy to count.
flow.context: This is the first step of the light-spreading test. You make a card with a small square window in it.

flow.do: 1. Stand the phone upright against a stack of books, with its torch facing along the table. 2. Switch the torch on. 3. Push the bottom edge of the card into a lump of dough, so it stands up. 4. Stand it 10 cm in front of the torch, with the hole level with the light.
flow.say: The torch is our Sun. The card lets through just a little square of its light. Let's keep both of them still from now on.
flow.kid: Stand the phone up with its torch on. Stand the card 10 cm in front of it. Line up the hole with the light.
flow.parent: Measure from the torch's light, on the back of the phone, to the card. The torch should shine straight through the middle of the hole.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess before you measure anything.
flow.say: Soon we'll catch the light on squared paper, first 20 cm from the torch and then 40 cm. 40 is twice as far as 20. At 40 cm, will the light cover the same number of squares, twice as many, or four times as many? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. At twice as far, will the light cover the same squares? Twice as many? Four times as many? Why?

good: Light spreads out, so it will cover more.
Twice as far, so twice as big.

flow.parent: Most children and many adults guess twice as many. Don't correct the guess. Let the counting answer it.

flow.do: 1. Tape the squared paper to a big book. 2. Stand the book 20 cm from the torch, facing it, so the light through the hole falls on the paper. 3. Measure how wide the lit square is. 4. Count the squares that are more than half lit. 5. Score the brightness 3, for bright.
flow.say: Here's the patch of light at 20 cm. How wide is it? How many squares does it cover? Let's count them together.
flow.kid: Put the paper 20 cm from the torch. Measure the lit square. Count the lit squares. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: The patch should be about 4 cm wide and cover about 16 squares. The edges are a little fuzzy, so count a square if more than half of it is lit. Your numbers may be a little different. That's fine.

flow.do: 1. Move the book back to 30 cm, then to 40 cm. 2. At each distance, measure the width of the lit square and count the squares. 3. Score how bright the patch looks: 2 for medium, 1 for dim.
flow.say: Now let's move the paper back. Look at the patch. Is it bigger? Is it brighter or dimmer?
flow.kid: Move the paper to 30 cm. Measure and count. Then 40 cm. Measure and count. Is it dimmer?

check.q: At 20 cm the light covered 16 squares. At 40 cm, twice as far, it covered about 64 squares. How many times as many squares is that?
options: The same number
2 times as many
4 times as many
check.why: 64 divided by 16 is 4. The patch was twice as wide and twice as tall, and 2 times 2 is 4. Picking '2 times as many' is the guess most people make. It would be right for a line of light, but a patch grows in two directions at once.

flow.parent: At 30 cm expect about 6 cm across and about 36 squares. At 40 cm, about 8 cm across and about 64 squares. If your counts are a bit off, look at the widths. They should go 4, 6, 8, growing in step with the distance.

flow.do: Ask your child what this means for each square.
flow.say: The same light came through the hole every time. At 40 cm, it was shared out over 4 times as many squares. So how much light did each square get?
flow.kid: The same light was shared out over 4 times as many squares. Did each square get more light or less?

ask.q: Why did the far patch look dimmer?
good: The same light was spread over more squares.
Each square got only a quarter of the light.

flow.do: Tell your child how this fits the planets.
flow.say: The Sun's light spreads out in just the same way. Jupiter is about 5 times as far from the Sun as the Earth is. 5 times 5 is 25. So sunlight there is about 25 times weaker. Neptune is about 30 times as far. 30 times 30 is 900. So Neptune gets about 900 times less sunlight than us.
flow.kid: Sunlight spreads out like the torch light. Neptune is 30 times as far as Earth. So Neptune gets 900 times less sunlight. It is very cold and dim there.

check.q: Mars is about one and a half times as far from the Sun as the Earth. What is sunlight like on Mars?
options: Stronger than on the Earth
The same as on the Earth
Weaker than on the Earth, a bit less than half as strong
check.why: Further from the Sun, the light is spread over more space, so it is weaker. One and a half times one and a half is a bit more than 2, so Mars gets a bit less than half our sunlight. Picking 'the same' means forgetting that light spreads out as it travels, which is what the squares showed.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: light gets weaker the further it travels. What I saw: at 20 cm the light covered 16 squares and was bright. At 40 cm it covered 64 squares and was dim. Why: the same light spreads over a bigger area, so each square gets less. That is why far planets are cold and dark.

experiments.title: The Marble and the Missing Rim: what keeps a planet going round?
experiments.question: When nothing pushes a rolling marble round any more, which way does it go?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A marble rolls round inside a ring, and then reaches a gap. Will it keep curving round, roll straight out from the middle, or roll straight on the way it was going? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same marble and the same ring every time. Start it in the same place and roll it with about the same speed. Roll it 5 times, because one roll can be a fluke.
results_table: Which way did it go? (kept curving, straight out from the middle, straight on)

materials.item: a paper plate about 20 to 25 cm across, or a strip of thin card 3 cm high and about 70 cm long
scissors and tape
a glass marble (goli)
a large sheet of newspaper, laid flat on a smooth floor or table
a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. Keep marbles away from children under 4, who could choke on them. Pick up the marble afterwards so nobody slips on it.

schedule.what: Make a ring with a gap. Guess where the marble goes at the gap. Roll it 5 times and draw its path.

experiments.record: Draw the ring from above, and draw the path the marble took after the gap. Write which guess was right.
experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a marble round inside a ring with a gap in it. You find out which way a moving thing goes when nothing turns it any more. The planets move in the same way.

setup.art: A paper plate seen from above with a quarter of its rim cut away, lying on a newspaper on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a quarter out of a paper plate's rim. Lay it on newspaper.

setup.art: A hand flicking a marble so it rolls fast round the inside of the plate's rim, with an arrow showing it going round.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the marble fast round the inside of the rim.

setup.art: The marble leaving the plate at the gap and rolling off in a straight line, with a pencil line drawn along its path on the newspaper.
setup.caption: 3. Watch where it goes at the gap. Draw its path.

flow.do: 1. Cut away about a quarter of the paper plate's rim, so the ring has a gap. 2. Lay the plate face up in the middle of the newspaper.
flow.say: This plate's rim will push a marble round in a circle. Then I'll cut a gap where the rim stops pushing.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a gap in the rim of the plate. Put the plate on the newspaper.
flow.parent: No paper plate? Bend a strip of thin card, 3 cm high, into three quarters of a circle about 25 cm across. Tape it down onto the newspaper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the marble test. You make a ring with a gap in it.

flow.do: 1. Show your child where the marble will leave the ring. 2. Ask for a guess, and a reason.
flow.say: The marble will roll round inside the rim. When it reaches the gap, which way will it go? Will it keep curving round, roll straight out from the middle, or roll straight on? Why?
flow.kid: Guess. At the gap, will the marble keep curving? Go straight out from the middle? Or go straight on? Why?

good: It was going round, so it keeps going round.
Nothing is holding it any more.

flow.parent: Many children, and many adults, guess that it keeps curving. That is a very natural idea. Let the marble answer.

flow.do: 1. Put the marble against the inside of the rim, far from the gap. 2. Flick it along the rim so it rolls fast all the way to the gap. 3. Watch where it goes. 4. Draw a pencil line on the newspaper along its path. 5. Do it 5 times.
flow.say: Let's roll it and watch closely. I'll draw its path each time.
flow.kid: Flick the marble round the inside of the rim. Watch where it goes at the gap. Draw its path. Try 5 times.
flow.parent: If the marble jumps over the rim, flick it a little more gently. It should roll off in a straight line along the way it was moving at the gap. It does not keep curving, and it does not roll straight out from the middle.

flow.do: Look at the 5 pencil lines together.
flow.say: Look at our lines. Did the marble keep curving, or go straight? So while it was going round, what was making it curve?
flow.kid: Look at your lines. Did the marble curve or go straight? What made it curve before?

check.q: While the marble went round, the rim pushed it inwards. What does the Sun do for the planets, like the rim did for the marble?
options: The Sun's gravity pulls each planet inwards, so its path keeps curving
The Sun pushes the planets along from behind
Nothing. Planets go round because they always have
check.why: The rim pushed the marble towards the middle, so it kept turning. At the gap, nothing pushed, and it went straight on. The Sun's gravity pulls each planet towards the Sun all the time, so its path keeps curving into an orbit. Picking 'nothing' is a natural guess, but the marble shows a moving thing goes straight unless a force turns it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a moving thing goes straight unless something turns it. What I saw: all 5 times, the marble rolled straight on at the gap. Why: the rim had been pushing it inwards. The Sun's gravity does that for the planets.

activities.title: Planet Line-up: how big is the Earth next to the others?

materials.item: a fist-sized lump of atta dough, or clay
old newspaper and tape, for the two biggest planets
a ruler or school scale
8 small paper labels and a pencil

activities.safety: Wash hands after playing with dough. Don't eat raw atta.

schedule.what: Guess the sizes. Make the eight planets to the same scale and line them up in order.

activities.record: Draw the line-up, with each planet's name and width in centimetres.
activities.context: In this activity you make the eight planets from dough and newspaper, all to the same scale, so you can see how big the Earth really is next to the others.

setup.art: A child rolling small balls of atta dough on a steel plate next to a ruler, with tiny paper labels.
setup.caption: 1. Roll dough balls for the small planets. Measure each one.

setup.art: Two balls of crumpled newspaper wrapped in tape, one 11 cm and one 9 cm across, next to the tiny dough balls.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze newspaper into balls for Jupiter and Saturn.

setup.art: All eight planets in a row on a table in order from the Sun, from a peppercorn-sized Mercury to a big newspaper Jupiter, with labels.
setup.caption: 3. Line them up in order and compare.

flow.do: 1. Roll a ball of dough 1 cm across. 2. Say this is the Earth. 3. Ask your child how big Jupiter would be at this size.
flow.say: This little ball is our Earth. If the Earth were this big, how big do you think Jupiter would be? As big as a pea? A lemon? A football?
flow.kid: This tiny ball is the Earth. Guess how big Jupiter would be. A pea? A lemon? A football?

good: Jupiter is the biggest planet.
It looks small in the sky, so maybe a bit bigger.

flow.context: This is the first step of the planet line-up. You start by guessing how big the other planets are next to the Earth.

flow.do: 1. Make Mercury 0.4 cm, about the size of a peppercorn. 2. Make Mars 0.5 cm. 3. Make Venus 1 cm, almost the same as the Earth. 4. Make Uranus and Neptune 4 cm each, about the size of a small lemon. 5. Label each one.
flow.say: Venus is almost a twin of the Earth. Mars is about half as wide. Mercury is smaller still. Now the two blue giants, Uranus and Neptune. Each is about 4 Earths wide.
flow.kid: Make Mercury tiny, like a peppercorn. Mars a bit bigger. Venus the same as Earth. Uranus and Neptune like small lemons.
flow.parent: Measure each ball against the ruler. The sizes don't need to be perfect. It's the comparison that matters.

flow.do: 1. Crumple newspaper and wrap it in tape into a ball 11 cm across. That is Jupiter. 2. Make another 9 cm across. That is Saturn. 3. Line up all eight in order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
flow.say: Jupiter is about 11 Earths wide. Saturn is about 9 Earths wide, without its rings. Let's put them all in order from the Sun.
flow.kid: Squeeze newspaper into a big ball for Jupiter. A bit smaller for Saturn. Put all eight in order.

check.q: Look at your line-up. Which planets are small and rocky, and which are giants?
options: The first four are small and rocky. The last four are giants.
They take turns: small, big, small, big.
They get bigger one by one, all the way out.
check.why: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small and rocky. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giants. Picking 'they get bigger one by one' is a good try at a pattern, but Uranus and Neptune are smaller than Jupiter and Saturn.

flow.do: Tell your child how big the Sun would be at the same scale.
flow.say: At this size, the Sun would be a ball 109 cm across. That's a bit more than a metre scale, and taller than our table. It would not fit through most doors sideways.
flow.kid: At this size, the Sun would be over a metre wide. Taller than the table! Measure it with your arms.

good: Jupiter is so much bigger than the Earth.
The Sun is bigger than everything put together.

activities.title: Galileo's Venus Test: a lamp, a ball and two ideas

materials.item: a lamp with no shade, or a phone torch standing upright, for the Sun
a light-coloured ball about the size of an orange, or an orange wrapped in white paper, for Venus
a dark room

activities.safety: A lamp bulb can get hot. A grown-up sets it up and keeps fingers off it.

schedule.what: Move a ball round a lamp and watch its shape and size change. Then try the old Earth-centred plan and see what is missing.

activities.record: Draw how Venus looked when it was near you and far from you.
activities.context: In this activity you repeat Galileo's test of 1610 with a lamp and a ball. You see why the changing shape of Venus showed that Venus goes round the Sun.

setup.art: A bare lamp glowing on a low table in a dark room, a child sitting on the floor about one and a half metres away.
setup.caption: 1. The lamp is the Sun. Sit about one and a half metres away.

setup.art: A grown-up carrying a white ball in a circle round the lamp, the ball fully lit on the far side and a big thin crescent on the near side.
setup.caption: 2. Carry the ball round the lamp. Watch its shape and size.

setup.art: The grown-up moving the ball in a small loop that always stays between the lamp and the child, showing only crescents.
setup.caption: 3. Try the old plan: Venus always between you and the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Put the lamp on a low table or stool. 2. Darken the room. 3. Your child sits on the floor about one and a half metres from the lamp, eyes about level with it.
flow.say: This lamp is the Sun. You are on the Earth. I will be Venus.
flow.kid: The lamp is the Sun. You are the Earth. Sit still and watch Venus.
flow.context: This is the first step of Galileo's Venus test. You set up a lamp as the Sun and sit back to watch.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball at arm's length from the lamp. 2. Walk slowly round the lamp in a circle, keeping the ball level with it. 3. Pause when the ball is nearest your child, and when it is to one side of the far side of the lamp.
flow.say: Watch the ball as I carry it round the Sun. How much of it is lit? Does it look bigger or smaller?
flow.kid: Watch the ball. How much is lit? Does it look big or small?

ask.q: What did Venus look like when it was nearest you?
good: Big, and only a thin crescent was lit.
Mostly dark.

ask.q: And on the far side of the Sun?
good: Small, and almost all lit up.

flow.parent: Keep the ball a little to one side when it is behind the lamp, so the lamp does not hide it.

flow.do: 1. Now act out the old Earth-centred plan. 2. Keep the ball always between the lamp and your child, moving it in a small loop there. 3. Ask what is missing.
flow.say: In the old plan, Venus always stays between the Earth and the Sun. Watch now. Can you ever see Venus fully lit?
flow.kid: Now Venus stays between you and the Sun. Can you ever see it fully lit?

check.q: Galileo saw Venus small and almost fully lit. What did that show?
options: Venus sometimes goes round to the far side of the Sun, so it goes round the Sun
Venus makes its own light
Venus always stays between the Earth and the Sun
check.why: Venus can only look fully lit when it is on the far side of the Sun from us. In the old plan, Venus never got there, so it could never look full. Picking 'Venus makes its own light' is a sensible guess, since Venus is so bright. But then it would always look full, and it does not.

flow.do: Talk about what Galileo found.
flow.say: In 1610 Galileo looked at Venus through his telescope for months. He saw these same changes. So Venus goes round the Sun, and the old plan was wrong.
flow.kid: Galileo saw Venus change like this in 1610. So Venus goes round the Sun!

ask.q: Why did he need a telescope?
good: Venus looks like a dot without one.
The shape is too small to see with just your eyes.

activities.title: Spot a Planet from Your Balcony

materials.item: a phone or computer with Stellarium Web (stellarium-web.org), a free sky map
a window, balcony or terrace with a view of the sky

activities.safety: On a terrace, a grown-up comes along and everyone stays away from the edge. Never look at the Sun.

schedule.what: Check which planets are up tonight. Find one from a window, balcony or terrace.

activities.record: Draw what you saw: the planet, anything near it, and which way you were facing.
activities.context: In this activity you find a real planet in the night sky. You are standing on one planet, looking at another.

setup.art: A child and a grown-up looking at a sky map on a phone, with planet names on the screen.
setup.caption: 1. Check which planets are up tonight on a sky map.

setup.art: A child on a city balcony at dusk pointing to one bright steady dot above buildings.
setup.caption: 2. Look in that direction for a bright dot that does not twinkle much.

flow.do: 1. Open Stellarium Web and let it find your location. 2. Look for Venus, Jupiter, Mars or Saturn above the horizon tonight. 3. Note which direction and how high.
flow.say: Let's see which planets are up tonight. Venus and Jupiter are the brightest, so they are easiest to see from a city.
flow.kid: Look at the sky map with your grown-up. Which planets are up tonight? Which way should you look?
flow.parent: Venus is only ever seen in the west after sunset or the east before sunrise. On some weeks no bright planet is up in the evening. Then try before sunrise, or come back in a few weeks.
flow.context: This is the first step of planet spotting. You use a free sky map to find out where to look.

flow.do: 1. Go to a window, balcony or terrace facing that way. 2. Look for a bright dot that shines steadily, without much twinkling. 3. Check it against the map.
flow.say: Planets shine steadily, while stars twinkle more. Can you find a bright, steady dot?
flow.kid: Find a bright dot that does not twinkle much. That is a planet!

flow.do: Ask your child what the planet's light is.
flow.say: That planet makes no light of its own. What are we seeing?
flow.kid: The planet makes no light. So what light are you seeing?

good: Sunlight bouncing off the planet.
Light from the Sun that hit the planet and came to us.

flow.think: Someone on that planet could look back and see the Earth as a bright dot. What would they think we are?

activities.title: The 3-Metre Solar System

materials.item: a string, rope or long strip of taped-together newspaper, 3 metres long
a measuring tape, or a school scale used again and again
9 paper labels and tape, or clothes pegs

activities.safety: Lay the string on the floor and pick it up afterwards so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Lay a 3-metre string along a corridor or hall. Mark the Sun and each planet at its real spacing.

activities.record: Draw the string with the Sun and the eight planets marked, and write each distance in centimetres.
activities.context: In this activity you lay out the distances of the planets from the Sun along a 3-metre string, all to the same scale. The Earth is 10 cm from the Sun.

setup.art: A 3-metre string laid along a flat's corridor floor, with a paper Sun label taped at one end.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the string along the floor. Tape the Sun label at one end.

setup.art: A child kneeling to tape planet labels close together near the Sun end, with a measuring tape beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Measure from the Sun and tape each planet's label.

setup.art: The whole string seen from one end, four labels bunched near the Sun and four spread far along it, Neptune at the far end.
setup.caption: 3. Stand at the Sun end and look along the string.

flow.do: 1. Lay the string straight along a corridor or across the hall. 2. Tape the Sun label at one end. 3. Ask your child to guess where the Earth goes, if Neptune is at the far end.
flow.say: The Sun is here, and Neptune is at the far end, 3 metres away. Where do you think the Earth goes?
flow.kid: The Sun is at this end. Neptune is at the far end. Where does the Earth go? Guess!
flow.context: This is the first step of the 3-metre solar system. You lay out a string and guess where the planets go.

flow.do: 1. Measure from the Sun end and tape each label: Mercury 4 cm, Venus 7 cm, Earth 10 cm, Mars 15 cm. 2. Then Jupiter 52 cm, Saturn 95 cm, Uranus 192 cm, Neptune 300 cm.
flow.say: At this scale, the Earth is just 10 cm from the Sun. Look how close the four rocky planets are. Now look how far the giants are.
flow.kid: Measure from the Sun. Tape each planet at its number. Earth goes at 10 cm.
flow.parent: These are real spacings, with 10 cm standing for the Earth's distance from the Sun. At this scale, the planets themselves would be far too small to see.

flow.do: 1. Stand at the Sun end and look along the string. 2. Ask what this means for sunlight.
flow.say: Remember the torch test? Sunlight spreads out as it goes. Which planets get the most sunlight? Which get almost none?
flow.kid: Remember the torch test? Which planets get lots of sunlight? Which get very little?

check.q: Saturn is about 10 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. How strong is sunlight on Saturn?
options: About 10 times weaker
About 100 times weaker
The same as on the Earth
check.why: Light spreads in two directions at once, so 10 times as far means 10 times 10, which is 100 times weaker. Picking '10 times weaker' forgets that the patch grows both wider and taller, as the squares in the torch test showed.

activities.title: How Old Would You Be on Mars?

materials.item: paper, a pencil and a phone calculator

schedule.what: Work out your age in Mercury years, Mars years and Jupiter years.

activities.record: Make a small table: planet, length of its year, and your age there.
activities.context: In this activity you work out how old you would be if you counted your birthdays on other planets, where a year is a different length.

setup.art: A child at a table with a notebook and a phone calculator, a drawing of Mercury, Earth and Mars beside the page.
setup.caption: 1. Work out how many days old you are.

setup.art: A small table in a notebook with three planets, their year lengths and the child's age on each.
setup.caption: 2. Divide by each planet's year to find your age there.

flow.do: 1. Multiply your child's age by 365 on the calculator. 2. Write down this number of days.
flow.say: A year on the Earth is about 365 days. You are 8, so you have lived about 8 times 365 days. That's 2,920 days.
flow.kid: Multiply your age by 365. That is about how many days you have lived.
flow.context: This is the first step of working out your age on other planets. You start by finding how many days old you are.

flow.do: 1. Divide the days by 88 for Mercury. 2. Divide by 687 for Mars. 3. For Jupiter, divide your age by 12.
flow.say: Mercury's year is only 88 days. Mars's year is 687 days. Jupiter's year is about 12 of ours. How old would you be on each?
flow.kid: Divide your days by 88 for Mercury. By 687 for Mars. How old are you there?

check.q: Divya, a girl in Class 3, is 8 years old on the Earth. Is she older or younger in Mars years?
options: Younger: about 4 Mars years old
Older: about 16 Mars years old
The same: 8 Mars years old
check.why: Mars takes longer than the Earth to go round the Sun, so its year is longer. Fewer long years fit into Divya's life: 2,920 days divided by 687 is about 4. Picking 'older' means thinking a longer orbit gives more birthdays, but it gives fewer.

projects.title: My Planet Guidebook

materials.item: 8 sheets of paper, folded and stapled into a booklet, or a thin notebook
colour pencils or crayons
your results from the torch test and the 3-metre string
a planet book from the library, or NASA Space Place on a phone

schedule.what: Make the booklet. Write and draw the pages for Mercury, Venus and Earth.
Write and draw the pages for Mars, Jupiter and Saturn.
Write and draw Uranus and Neptune. Add a last page: 'Why I'm glad I live on the Earth'.

projects.record: The finished guidebook, with one page for each planet.
projects.context: In this 3-day project you make a guidebook for travellers, with one page for each planet. Each page says what a visitor would find there.

setup.art: Eight sheets of paper folded and stapled into a small booklet, with 'My Planet Guidebook' written on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and staple 8 sheets into a booklet.

setup.art: An open booklet page with a drawing of Mars and four short lines: distance, size, year, and 'What a visitor would see'.
setup.caption: 2. Give each planet a page with four facts and a drawing.

setup.art: A child showing the finished booklet to a grandmother, open on the Earth page with a blue planet and a fish.
setup.caption: 3. Read your guidebook to someone at home.

flow.do: 1. Fold 8 sheets in half and staple them at the fold. 2. Write a title on the cover. 3. Write one planet name at the top of each page, in order.
flow.say: Let's make a guidebook for space travellers. One page for each planet, in order from the Sun.
flow.kid: Fold and staple your booklet. Write one planet name on each page, in order.
flow.context: This is the first step of the planet guidebook project. You make the booklet and plan the pages.

flow.do: 1. On each page, write four short lines. How far from the Sun, compared with the Earth. How wide, compared with the Earth. How long its year is. One thing a visitor would see. 2. Draw the planet.
flow.say: Use your string and your dough planets to help. What would a visitor see on Venus? Thick yellow clouds, and terrible heat.
flow.kid: Write four facts on each page. How far. How wide. How long a year. What a visitor sees. Then draw it.
flow.wait: Do three planets a day, over three days.

flow.do: 1. On each page, add how strong the sunlight is, compared with the Earth. 2. Use the torch-test rule: times the distance by itself.
flow.say: Jupiter is 5 times as far. 5 times 5 is 25. So sunlight there is 25 times weaker. Let's add that to each page.
flow.kid: Add how weak the sunlight is. Times the distance by itself. Jupiter is 5, so 25 times weaker.
flow.parent: Use about 7 times stronger for Mercury, 2 times stronger for Venus, half as strong for Mars, 25 times weaker for Jupiter, 100 times weaker for Saturn, 400 times weaker for Uranus and 900 times weaker for Neptune. These are rounded.

flow.do: 1. Add a last page: 'Why I'm glad I live on the Earth'. 2. Your child reads the guidebook aloud to someone at home.
flow.say: Now the last page. After visiting all eight, why are you glad to live on the Earth?
flow.kid: Write the last page. Why are you glad to live on the Earth? Read your book to someone.

ask.q: Why is the Earth a good place to live?
good: It has liquid water.
It is not too hot or too cold.
It has air we can breathe.

challenges.title: Sunlight for a Spacecraft Going to Jupiter
challenges.problem: A spacecraft runs on sunlight. Near the Earth, a solar panel 1 square big gives it all the power it needs. Design solar panels that give the same power at Mars, at Jupiter and at Saturn.
constraints: Use squared paper: 1 square is the panel the spacecraft needs near the Earth.
Use the torch-test rule: times the distance by itself to find how much weaker the sunlight is.
Your panels must fold up to fit inside a rocket, which is about 5 squares wide.
general: Make the panels bigger, in step with how weak the sunlight is. Jupiter is about 5 times as far, so the panel must be about 25 squares, 5 by 5.
Fold the panels like a fan or a map, so they open out in space.
Some spacecraft going very far, like Voyager 1 and 2, do not use sunlight at all. They carry a nuclear power source instead.
creative: Use curved mirrors to gather extra sunlight onto a smaller panel.
Make the panels out of long thin strips that unroll, like a mat.
Point the panels straight at the Sun, because light that hits a panel at a slant is spread over more of it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own folding panel for Saturn. Saturn is about 10 times as far as the Earth. How many squares do you need? How will it fold up to fit in the rocket?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You use what the torch test showed to plan solar panels for a spacecraft travelling far from the Sun.

setup.art: A single square of paper labelled 'Earth: 1 square', next to a 5 by 5 square labelled 'Jupiter: 25 squares'.
setup.caption: 1. Work out how many squares each planet needs.

setup.art: A child folding a big sheet of squared paper like a fan, so it fits inside a narrow paper rocket.
setup.caption: 2. Make the panel fold up to fit inside the rocket.

flow.do: 1. Remind your child of the torch test. 2. Ask how big a panel must be at Jupiter, 5 times as far as the Earth.
flow.say: Remember the torch test? Twice as far, four times the squares. Jupiter is 5 times as far. How many squares must the panel be?
flow.kid: Jupiter is 5 times as far. How many squares of panel do you need? Times 5 by 5.
flow.context: This is the first step of the spacecraft panel challenge. You work out how big a panel must be far from the Sun.

flow.do: 1. Cut out panels for Mars (about 2 squares), Jupiter (25 squares) and Saturn (about 90 squares). 2. Fold each so it fits inside a rocket 5 squares wide.
flow.say: Real spacecraft have this problem. Juno, which reached Jupiter in 2016, has three solar panels, each about 9 metres long.
flow.kid: Cut out a panel for each planet. Fold each one to fit in a rocket 5 squares wide.
flow.parent: Mars is about one and a half times as far, and one and a half times one and a half is about 2. Saturn is about 9 and a half times as far, so about 90 squares.

flow.do: Ask your child to show the folded panels and explain the plan.
flow.say: Show me how your Saturn panel opens out. Why does it need to be so big?
flow.kid: Show your folded panel. Open it out. Say why it is so big.

ask.q: Why can't one square of panel work at Saturn?
good: Sunlight is about 90 times weaker there.
The light is spread out over many more squares.

challenges.title: Keep an Ice Cube Cool in the Sunshine
challenges.problem: A spacecraft flying close to the Sun gets very hot. Design a sunshade that keeps an ice cube from melting in strong sunlight for as long as possible.
constraints: The shade must not touch the ice cube.
Test it next to an ice cube with no shade, both in the same sunny spot.
materials: 2 ice cubes of the same size
card, aluminium foil, white paper and black paper
general: Hold a piece of card between the Sun and the ice cube, so it sits in shadow.
Cover the side of the card that faces the Sun with white paper or foil, so it bounces back sunlight.
Leave a gap of air between the shade and the ice cube.
creative: Use two layers of card with an air gap between them.
Tilt the shade so it bounces sunlight away rather than soaking it up.
The Parker Solar Probe, launched in 2018, flies closer to the Sun than anything before it. Its shield has a white front facing the Sun. Find out what is inside it.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sunshade, test it against an unshaded ice cube, and time how long each takes to melt.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about keeping something cool in strong sunlight, the problem every spacecraft near the Sun has to solve.

setup.art: Two ice cubes on two steel saucers on a sunny windowsill, one with a card shade covered in foil standing over it.
setup.caption: 1. Put two ice cubes in the sun. Shade one of them.

setup.art: One ice cube melted into a puddle and the shaded one still mostly solid, with a clock showing 20 minutes later.
setup.caption: 2. Check every 5 minutes. Which melts first?

flow.do: 1. Put two ice cubes of the same size on two saucers. 2. Put both in the same sunny spot. 3. Ask your child to guess how much longer a shaded one will last.
flow.say: Close to the Sun, spacecraft get hotter and hotter. Let's see if we can protect an ice cube. Which will melt first?
flow.kid: Put two ice cubes in the sun. Guess which will melt first, and why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ice cube challenge. You put two ice cubes in sunshine to compare.

flow.do: 1. Build a shade from card and foil or white paper over one ice cube, not touching it. 2. Check both every 5 minutes. 3. Write down when each one has melted.
flow.say: Let's build our shade. The shiny or white side faces the Sun. Then we check every 5 minutes.
flow.kid: Build a shade over one ice cube. Don't touch the ice. Check every 5 minutes.
flow.parent: On a hot afternoon, the bare ice cube may melt in about 15 to 30 minutes. If the sun goes behind a cloud, keep going. Both ice cubes are in the same light, so the test is still fair.

flow.do: Talk about the results.
flow.say: Which one lasted longer? Why does the shade work? What does this tell us about Mercury, so close to the Sun?
flow.kid: Which ice cube lasted longer? Why? What would happen on Mercury?

ask.q: Why did the shaded ice cube last longer?
good: The shade stopped the sunlight reaching it.
The white side bounced sunlight away.
