quiz.p: Which planet is third from the Sun?
quiz.why: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars. The Earth is third. Picking Mars is close: Mars is fourth, just past us.

quiz.p: How many planets go round the Sun?
quiz.why: There are eight planets. Picking nine is what books said before 2006, when Pluto was counted. Picking five comes from the planets you can see without a telescope.

quiz.p: Why is Pluto now called a dwarf planet, not a planet?
opts: It shares its path round the Sun with many other icy worlds
It stopped going round the Sun
quiz.why: Since 2006, a planet must clear its path. Pluto is round and goes round the Sun, but many other icy worlds share its path. Picking 'not round' is a good guess for small worlds, but Pluto is round.

quiz.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3, moves the squared paper from 20 cm to 40 cm from a phone torch. What happens to the patch of light?
opts: It covers about four times as many squares and looks dimmer
It covers twice as many squares and looks just as bright
quiz.why: Twice as far, the patch is twice as wide and twice as tall, so four times the squares. The same light is shared over more squares, so it is dimmer. Picking 'twice as many' grows it only one way.

quiz.p: Neptune is about 30 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. What does that mean for Neptune?
opts: Its sunlight is about 900 times weaker, so it is very cold and dim
Its sunlight is just 30 times weaker
It gets more sunlight because it is bigger
It is as warm as the Earth
quiz.why: 30 times 30 is 900, so sunlight there is about 900 times weaker. Picking '30 times weaker' forgets that light spreads out in two directions at once.

quiz.p: Why does Mercury take only 88 days to go round the Sun, while the Earth takes 365?
opts: Mercury is closer, so it has a shorter path and moves faster
quiz.why: Closer to the Sun, the path is shorter and the Sun's gravity is stronger, so the planet moves faster. Picking 'Mercury is bigger' is wrong twice: Mercury is the smallest planet, and size does not set the year.

quiz.p: A marble rolls round inside a plate's rim. At a gap in the rim, which way does it go?
opts: Straight on, the way it was moving
quiz.why: With nothing pushing it inwards, the marble goes straight on. The Sun's gravity is what keeps bending a planet's path. Picking 'keeps curving' is a very common idea, but the marble test shows it is not what happens.

quiz.p: Through his telescope in 1610, Galileo saw Venus look small and almost fully lit. What did this show?
opts: Venus is bigger than the Sun
quiz.why: Venus can only look fully lit when it is on the far side of the Sun from us. So it must go round the Sun. Picking 'makes its own light' does not fit: then Venus would always look full.

quiz.p: Before Galileo, most astronomers in Europe thought what?
opts: The Earth stood still in the centre and everything went round it
The Earth went round the Moon
quiz.why: Most followed Ptolemy's Earth-centred plan for about 1,500 years. Galileo's view of Venus showed it was wrong.

quiz.p: Which of these is a giant planet with no solid ground?
quiz.why: Saturn is a giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium gas. Mars, Mercury and Venus are rocky planets you could stand on.

quiz.p: What do the four rocky planets have in common?
opts: They are small, have hard ground, and are the four nearest the Sun
They are all bigger than Jupiter
quiz.why: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small, rocky and close to the Sun. Only the Earth has liquid water on its surface today.

quiz.p: What makes the Earth a planet?
opts: It is a big round world that goes round the Sun and has cleared its path
It has people living on it
quiz.why: A planet is round, goes round the Sun and has cleared its path. The Earth does all three. Having a moon or people is not part of the rule, and planets do not make their own light.

items.p: Put the eight planets in order, starting with the one nearest the Sun.
items.why: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The sentence 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' helps. A strong answer puts the Earth third.

items.p: Sort the planets into rocky planets and giant planets.
items.a: see items
items.why: The four nearest the Sun are small and rocky. The four furthest are giants made mostly of gas, or gas and ice. A strong answer notices that the two kinds are in two groups, not mixed up.

items.p: Anu, a girl in Class 3, says, 'The Earth is not a planet. Planets are the dots up in the sky.' Is she right?
items.why: False. The Earth goes round the Sun, like the other seven planets, so it is a planet too. From Mars, the Earth looks like a bright dot in the sky. A strong answer says the Earth only looks different because we are standing on it.

items.p: In the torch test, the patch of light covered 16 squares when the paper was 20 cm away. About how many squares did it cover at 40 cm?
items.why: Twice as far, the patch is twice as wide and twice as tall, so it covers 2 times 2, which is 4 times as many squares. 4 times 16 is 64. Picking 32 is the most common mistake: it doubles only one way.

items.p: In the torch test, the far patch of light looked dimmer than the near one. The torch was the same. Explain why.
items.a: The same amount of light came through the hole each time. Far away, it was spread over more squares, so each square got less light and looked dimmer.
items.why: A strong answer says the light was not used up. It was shared out over a bigger area.

items.p: The path a planet takes as it goes round the Sun is called its ____.
items.why: An orbit is the path one thing takes round another. The Earth's orbit round the Sun takes one year.

items.p: What keeps the Earth going round the Sun?
opts: The Sun's gravity pulls the Earth inwards while the Earth moves forwards
The Earth is tied to the Sun by an invisible string
Nothing. The Earth is not moving
items.why: The Earth moves forwards very fast, and the Sun's gravity keeps bending its path round. Picking 'wind' is a creative guess, but space has almost no air, so there is no wind. The marble test showed that without a force pulling inwards, a moving thing goes straight.

items.p: Draw the Sun and the first four planets, with the Earth in the right place. Draw an arrow to show which way the Sun's gravity pulls the Earth.
items.a: The Sun, then Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars in order, with an arrow from the Earth pointing towards the Sun.
items.why: Gravity pulls the Earth towards the Sun, not along its path. A strong drawing puts the Earth third and points the arrow at the Sun.
items.art: An empty space with a small Sun drawn at the left edge.

items.p: Match each planet to something true about it.
pairs: the smallest planet, nearest the Sun
the hottest planet, with thick clouds
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These are the best-known facts about each planet. A strong answer could also say why Venus is hottest: its thick air traps heat.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi, Meera and Sana, are arguing about Pluto.

views.says: Pluto is a planet. It is round, it has moons, and it goes round the Sun.
Pluto is a dwarf planet. It shares its path with lots of other icy worlds, so it has not cleared its path.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the 2006 rule or Pluto's features as evidence. It also gives the other side its due. Meera is right that Pluto is round and has moons. Sana is right that the 2006 rule says a planet must clear its path.
items.why: This is a real argument among astronomers. It is about where to draw the line around the word 'planet', so both sides have good reasons.

items.p: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, so it must be the hottest planet.
items.why: False. Venus is hotter, about 460 degrees Celsius, because its thick air traps heat like a blanket. Mercury has almost no air, so its heat escapes. A strong answer names Venus and says why.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: The Sun is a star. It makes its own light. Mars, Jupiter and the Earth are planets. They shine only with sunlight that falls on them.

items.p: Why can the Earth have rivers and rain, when Mercury and Neptune cannot?
items.a: The Earth is at a distance from the Sun where water stays liquid. Mercury is so close that water would boil away. Neptune is so far that water freezes solid.
items.why: A strong answer links the distance to how strong the sunlight is, as the torch test showed.

items.p: Label the picture of the solar system: the Sun, the Earth, Jupiter, and the asteroid belt.
items.a: The Sun in the middle, the Earth on the third orbit, the asteroid belt between the fourth and fifth orbits, and Jupiter on the fifth orbit.
items.why: The asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter. A strong answer counts the orbits out from the Sun.
items.art: The Sun with eight orbits drawn round it, a ring of dots between the fourth and fifth orbits, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Which planet takes the longest to go round the Sun once?
items.why: Neptune is furthest from the Sun. It has the longest path and moves slowest, so its year is about 165 Earth years. Picking Jupiter means thinking the biggest planet is the slowest, but size does not set a planet's year.

items.p: Jupiter is about 5 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. How strong is sunlight at Jupiter?
opts: About 5 times weaker than on the Earth
About 25 times weaker than on the Earth
About 5 times stronger than on the Earth
The same as on the Earth
items.why: Light spreads out wider and taller at the same time. 5 times as far means 5 times 5, which is 25 times weaker. Picking '5 times weaker' is the usual first guess, but the torch test showed the patch grows both ways.

items.p: In the marble test, the marble went straight on at the gap. What would happen to the Earth if the Sun's gravity suddenly stopped? Explain using the marble test.
items.a: The Earth would fly off in a straight line, the way it was moving at that moment. The rim pushed the marble inwards. At the gap, the push stopped, and the marble went straight on. The Sun's gravity is like the rim for the Earth.
items.why: A strong answer says the Earth would go straight, not fall into the Sun and not keep curving.

items.p: If you could stand on Jupiter, you would stand on solid ground made of gas.
items.why: False. Jupiter has no solid surface to stand on. Going down, its gas just gets thicker and hotter. A strong answer says Jupiter is a giant planet made mostly of gas.

items.p: Galileo saw Venus look small and fully lit, and at other times big and a thin crescent. Explain why this showed that Venus goes round the Sun.
items.a: Venus can only look fully lit when it is on the far side of the Sun from us, where its whole lit half faces us. It looks small there because it is far away. If Venus always stayed between the Earth and the Sun, we would only see crescents.
items.why: A strong answer links 'fully lit' to 'on the far side of the Sun', and links 'small' to 'far away'.

items.p: Put these planets in order from the shortest year to the longest year.
items.why: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year. So the order of years is the same as the order of distance.

items.p: Venus is about the same size as the Earth and close to us. Why can nothing live on its surface as far as we know?
opts: Its thick air traps so much heat that the ground is about 460 degrees Celsius
It has no sunlight at all
It is made of gas with no ground
It is too cold, like Neptune
items.why: Venus gets about twice our sunlight, and its very thick air traps the heat. Picking 'no sunlight' forgets that Venus is closer to the Sun than we are. Picking 'too cold' forgets the trapped heat.

items.p: Pluto has been called a ____ planet since 2006.
items.why: In 2006 the world group of astronomers decided that a planet must clear its path. Pluto shares its path, so it is a dwarf planet.

items.p: Kavitha, a girl in Class 4, says, 'The torch light ran out as it travelled, like water draining away. That's why the far patch was dim.' Is she right? What really happened?
items.a: She is not right. The light did not run out. The same amount of light reached the paper, but it was spread over more squares. So each square got less, and the patch looked dimmer.
items.why: A strong answer uses the square counts as evidence: 16 squares bright, 64 squares dim, the same light.

items.p: In the 3-metre solar system, the Earth was 10 cm from the Sun and Neptune was 300 cm. What did the model show about the planets?
opts: The four rocky planets are bunched close to the Sun, and the giants are spread far out
The giants are closest to the Sun
Neptune is just 3 times as far as the Earth
items.why: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all fit in the first 15 cm. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are spread over nearly 3 metres. Picking 'spaced evenly' is how many books draw it, but books squeeze the planets to fit the page.

items.p: Mars is red because it is very hot, like a glowing coal.
items.why: False. Mars is colder than the Earth. Its red colour comes from rusty iron in its rocks and dust. A strong answer says what the red really is.

items.p: A year on Mars is 687 Earth days. Is a child who is 8 on the Earth older or younger in Mars years? Explain.
items.a: Younger. A Mars year is almost twice as long as an Earth year, so fewer Mars years have passed. 8 years is about 2,920 days, and 2,920 divided by 687 is about 4. So the child is about 4 in Mars years.
items.why: A strong answer explains that a longer year means fewer birthdays, and shows the working.

items.p: Look at your dough planet line-up. Write two things you noticed about the sizes of the planets.
items.a: For example: Jupiter is about 11 times as wide as the Earth. Venus is almost the same size as the Earth. Mercury is the smallest. The giants are all much bigger than the rocky planets.
items.why: A strong answer uses numbers from the line-up, not just 'big' and 'small'.

items.p: Two people talk about the solar system long ago.

views.who: Ptolemy, an astronomer in Egypt about 150 CE
views.says: The Earth stands still. We do not feel it move, and the Sun, Moon and planets all cross our sky.
Venus shows a full set of phases through my telescope. That can only happen if Venus goes round the Sun.

items.ask: Who do you think had the better evidence? Explain why. Then say what Ptolemy got right about what we see.
items.a: A strong answer says Galileo's evidence was better, because the phases of Venus could not happen in Ptolemy's plan. It also says Ptolemy was right that the sky looks as if it moves round us, and that we don't feel the Earth move.
items.why: Ptolemy's plan fitted what people saw with their eyes for 1,500 years. New evidence from a telescope showed it was wrong. Good scientists change their minds when the evidence changes.

items.p: Draw the patch of light in the torch test at 20 cm and at 40 cm, side by side, on squared paper.
items.a: A 4 by 4 square at 20 cm and an 8 by 8 square at 40 cm, with the second one shaded lighter.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the far patch twice as wide and twice as tall, covering four times as many squares, and paler.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the path of a planet round the Sun
the force that pulls things towards each other
the time a planet takes to go round the Sun once
a tube that makes faraway things look bigger
the layer of air round a planet
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Uranus is about 19 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Work out about how many times weaker sunlight is at Uranus. Show your working.
items.a: 19 times 19 is 361. So sunlight at Uranus is about 360 times weaker than on the Earth.
items.why: A strong answer uses the torch-test rule, times the distance by itself, and shows the multiplication.

items.p: Three people talk about why life is found on the Earth.

views.says: Distance matters most. The Earth is at the right distance from the Sun for liquid water.
Air matters most. Venus is not far from the right distance, but its thick air makes it far too hot.
We cannot be sure yet. We know only one planet with life, so we do not know everything life needs.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Use evidence from this unit. Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks one view and backs it with evidence: the torch test and Neptune's weak sunlight for Revathi, Venus's thick air for Farhan, or the fact that we know only one living planet for Shalini. It also gives another view its due.
items.why: All three have a point. Distance sets how much sunlight arrives, air decides how much heat stays, and with only one example of life, nobody can be sure what matters most.

items.p: Which planet would a spacecraft need the biggest solar panels for?
items.why: Neptune is furthest from the Sun, so sunlight there is weakest, about 900 times weaker than at the Earth. A panel there would need to be about 900 times bigger to collect the same light. Picking Jupiter is right that it is far, but Neptune is much further.

items.p: Saturn is about 10 times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Imagine the torch test with the paper 10 times as far away. How many times as many squares would the light cover? Explain.
items.a: 100 times as many. The patch would be 10 times as wide and 10 times as tall, and 10 times 10 is 100.
items.why: A strong answer applies the two-directions rule to a new distance, and links it to Saturn getting about 100 times less sunlight.

items.p: Many old books called the Sun and the Moon planets. Today we do not. Give one reason the Sun is not a planet, and one reason the Moon is not a planet.
items.a: The Sun makes its own light, so it is a star, and the planets go round it. The Moon goes round the Earth, not straight round the Sun, so it is a moon.
items.why: A strong answer uses what a planet is: a round world that goes round the Sun and does not make its own light.

items.p: Ravi, a boy in Class 4, says, 'If the Sun's gravity pulls the planets in, they should all fall into the Sun.' Why don't they?
items.a: The planets are moving forwards very fast. Gravity pulls them inwards, but their forward motion carries them past. Together, these bend their paths into orbits, so they keep going round instead of falling in.
items.why: A strong answer names both parts: the forward motion and the inward pull. Ravi has noticed something true: if a planet stopped moving forwards, it would fall into the Sun.

items.p: Leela, a girl in Class 4, does the torch test with the paper at 10 cm and then at 30 cm. How many times as many squares does the light cover at 30 cm?
items.why: 30 cm is 3 times as far as 10 cm. The patch is 3 times as wide and 3 times as tall, and 3 times 3 is 9. Picking '3 times as many' grows the patch in only one direction.

items.p: In 1846, astronomers found Neptune by working out where it must be before they looked. What clue did they use?
opts: Uranus was being tugged off its expected path by something
Neptune's light was shining on Uranus
items.why: Uranus was not moving quite as expected. Urbain Le Verrier worked out that the gravity of an unseen planet could explain it, and said where to look. Johann Galle found Neptune almost exactly there. Picking 'Neptune's light' forgets that Neptune is far too dim to light anything.

items.p: Why are the four planets near the Sun rocky, while the four far out are giants?
opts: Near the young Sun it was too warm for ice, so only rock and metal could clump. Further out, ice froze too, so planets grew bigger and gathered gas
The giants were pushed out by the Sun's wind
Rocky planets are older than giant planets
Nobody has any idea at all
items.why: This is the best explanation scientists have. Near the Sun, only rock and metal stayed solid. Further out, ice could freeze as well, so there was more material, and big cores pulled in lots of gas. Picking 'nobody has any idea' is too strong: the details are still studied, but the main idea has good evidence.

items.p: Plan an investigation. Your friend thinks a white ball and a black ball would look the same in the torch light. How would you test it fairly? What would you keep the same?
items.a: Put each ball the same distance from the same torch, in a dark room, one at a time. Keep the torch, the distance and the room the same. Only change the colour of the ball. Then compare how bright each ball looks.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing and names at least two things kept the same. Planets differ in colour too: icy, cloudy Venus reflects much more sunlight than dark rocky Mercury.

items.p: The Earth moves at about 30 kilometres every second as it goes round the Sun. Why don't we feel this?
opts: We, our homes and the air all move along with the Earth, smoothly and steadily
The Earth is really standing still
We are too heavy to feel it
items.why: We feel a change in speed, like a bus braking, not steady motion. Everything around us moves with the Earth. Picking 'the Earth is standing still' is what people believed for thousands of years, until the evidence showed otherwise.

items.p: Astronomers voted in 2006 that a planet must clear its path. Pluto did not change at all. Did Pluto stop being a planet, or did people change a word? Explain what you think.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. A strong answer sees that Pluto itself stayed the same, and that people changed the rule for the word 'planet'. It may say why a clear rule is useful, or why some astronomers still prefer the old one.
items.why: This question is about the difference between a thing and the name we give it. There is no single right answer, but a strong one gives a reason.

items.p: Draw what the Earth and the Moon might look like from Mars, through a small telescope. Label which is which.
items.a: Two dots side by side, a bigger blue-white one labelled Earth and a smaller grey one labelled Moon, both lit on the same side.
items.why: From Mars, the Earth and the Moon are two small lit dots. Both are lit by the Sun from the same side. A strong drawing shows the Earth bigger and brighter.

items.p: On Neptune at noon, the Sun would look like a dazzling tiny star.
items.why: True. Neptune is about 30 times as far as the Earth, so the Sun looks about 30 times smaller across. It is still much brighter than any other star, because it is so much nearer than them.

items.p: Sort these into planets, dwarf planets and other things that go round the Sun.
items.a: see items
items.why: The Earth and Neptune are planets. Pluto and Ceres are round but share their paths, so they are dwarf planets. Most asteroids and comets are too small to be round.

applications: Planning spacecraft journeys, like India's Mangalyaan to Mars in 2014, uses the orbits of the planets.
Solar panels on spacecraft are sized using how sunlight weakens with distance.
Lighting engineers use the same rule: a lamp twice as high lights the floor a quarter as brightly.
Calendars count the Earth's trips round the Sun as years.
Searching for life beyond the Earth starts with places that may have liquid water.
Weather satellites and space telescopes are placed in orbits worked out from gravity.

maths.problem: In the torch test, the patch of light was 4 cm wide at 20 cm and 8 cm wide at 40 cm. How many 1 cm squares does each patch cover? How many times as many does the far one cover?
maths.answer: 16 squares and 64 squares. The far one covers 4 times as many.
maths.explain: A patch 4 cm wide and 4 cm tall covers 4 times 4, which is 16 squares. A patch 8 cm wide and 8 cm tall covers 8 times 8, which is 64 squares. 64 divided by 16 is 4. So the far patch covers 4 times as many squares.
maths.why_maths: Counting the squares, or multiplying the sides, shows exactly how much more space the same light has to cover.
maths.context: This is about the torch test, where you shone a phone torch through a square hole onto squared paper.

maths.problem: Sunlight gets weaker by the distance times itself. Mars is about 1 and a half times as far from the Sun as the Earth. Jupiter is about 5 times as far. Neptune is about 30 times as far. Work out how many times weaker sunlight is at Jupiter and at Neptune.
maths.answer: About 25 times weaker at Jupiter, and about 900 times weaker at Neptune.
maths.explain: 5 times 5 is 25. 30 times 30 is 900. Mars is harder: 1 and a half times 1 and a half is 2 and a quarter, so about 2 times weaker.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying turns a distance into how strong the sunlight is, so you can predict how cold and dim a planet will be.
maths.context: This uses the rule from the torch test: twice as far, four times weaker.

maths.problem: In the 3-metre solar system, the Earth is 10 cm from the Sun and Neptune is 300 cm. How many times as far from the Sun is Neptune? Jupiter is at 52 cm. About how many times as far as the Earth is that?
maths.answer: Neptune is 30 times as far. Jupiter is about 5 times as far.
maths.explain: 300 divided by 10 is 30. 52 divided by 10 is a little over 5. So Jupiter is about 5 times as far as the Earth.
maths.why_maths: A scale model lets us see huge distances in a corridor. Dividing tells us how many Earth-distances each planet is.
maths.context: This is about the 3-metre solar system, where you laid out the planets along a string.

maths.problem: A year on Mercury is 88 days. A year on Venus is 225 days. Arjun, a boy who is 6, has lived about 2,190 days. About how many Mercury years is that? About how many Venus years?
maths.answer: About 25 Mercury years and about 10 Venus years.
maths.explain: 2,190 divided by 88 is about 24.9, so about 25 Mercury years. 2,190 divided by 225 is about 9.7, so about 10 Venus years. A shorter year means more birthdays.
maths.why_maths: Dividing a life into years of different lengths shows how a planet's distance from the Sun changes the length of its year.
maths.context: This is about counting birthdays on other planets, where a year is a different length.

maths.problem: The Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun. Neptune is about 30 times as far. About how far from the Sun is Neptune?
maths.answer: About 4,500 million kilometres, which is 4.5 billion kilometres.
maths.explain: 150 times 30 is 4,500. So Neptune is about 4,500 million kilometres from the Sun.
maths.why_maths: Space distances are huge. Using the Earth's distance as a measuring stick makes them easier to work with.
maths.context: This is about the real distances of the planets from the Sun.

roots.context: We have met the eight planets and measured how light spreads out. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the torch test, twice as far meant the same light spread over four times as many squares. The Sun's light spreads the same way, out to all eight planets. Neptune is 30 times further from the Sun than Earth, so sunlight there is about 900 times weaker. Earth's warmth, rain and plant food all run on the share of sunlight that reaches Earth's distance.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about 'the Earth' and 'the planets' as if the Earth were a different kind of thing, and as if its warmth were its own. But the Earth stands in the same sunlight as the other seven planets. What makes it warm, wet and living is mostly the share of that light its distance gives it.
deep_truth.evidence: At 20 cm the torch light covered 16 squares and was bright. At 40 cm the same light covered 64 squares and was dim. Spacecraft measure sunlight weakening in exactly this way as they fly out from the Sun.

three.who_am_i: You live on a planet. The warmth on your skin and the food on your plate began as sunlight that travelled to the Earth.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing we know of lives on the Earth, at a distance from the Sun where water stays liquid.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth is one of eight planets sharing one Sun. Each gets a different share of its light.

roots.thread: One Sun sends out its light in every direction. The same light reaches all eight planets, but at each distance it is spread thinner. That one difference, along with what each planet is made of and how much air it has, gives eight very different worlds: scorched Mercury, cloud-wrapped Venus, blue Earth, red Mars and the cold, dim giants. On the Earth, the share of sunlight we get drives the wind and rain and feeds every plant. So one source of light becomes many worlds and, on one of them, countless living things.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The torch test uses a phone torch, because its light is a small bright point. A big torch with a shiny reflector sends its light out in a beam and will not give a clean result, so the materials ask for a phone. With the card 10 cm from the torch and a 2 cm hole, the patch is 4 cm wide at 20 cm, 6 cm at 30 cm and 8 cm at 40 cm, which is easy to measure. The edges are fuzzy by a few millimetres, so the step says to count squares more than half lit and to check the widths. The room must be dark, so evening is best. The marble test works on a smooth floor or table. If there is no paper plate, a bent strip of card taped to newspaper works. The Venus test needs a lamp without a shade, or a phone torch, and the ball must be kept a little to one side behind the lamp. Planet spotting depends on the season, so it is outside the spine and says what to do if no planet is up. The ice cube challenge needs sunshine, and gives what to do if the sun goes in. Both games work with two players, and Which Planet Am I? works alone. The spine is the intro, the planet line-up, the torch test, the explanations, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes over two sessions.

how_we_found_out.story: For about 1,500 years, most astronomers in Europe and the Middle East followed Ptolemy, who lived in Egypt about 150 CE. He taught that the Earth stands still in the centre, and the Sun and planets go round it. In his plan, Venus always stays between the Earth and the Sun. If that were true, we would only ever see Venus as a thin crescent or a dark disc, never fully lit. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus said the planets, the Earth among them, go round the Sun, but nobody could yet show who was right. In 1610 Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, turned his new telescope on Venus. Over many months he watched her change. When Venus was on the far side of the Sun, she looked small and almost round, fully lit. As she came closer, she grew bigger and thinner, into a large crescent. Venus could only be fully lit if she went round to the far side of the Sun. So Venus goes round the Sun, not the Earth, and Ptolemy's plan was wrong. Later measurements showed that the Earth goes round the Sun too.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, building on the work of Nicolaus Copernicus
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The Earth is the still centre, and everything in the sky goes round it, with Venus always between the Earth and the Sun. Galileo saw Venus fully lit and small, which can only happen if Venus goes round the Sun.
